n: This revelation was recorded July 12, 1843, in Nauvoo, though Joseph Smith had learned some of its principles years earlier while translating the Bible. It begins with his question: how were Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, David, and Solomon justified in having multiple wives?

f.g: Joseph likely asked around 1831 while revising the Old Testament (JST); the revelation was written down in 1843 at Hyrum Smith’s request.
In the Old Testament, legal wives of secondary status, not illicit partners.

n: The Lord promises to answer the question.

f.g: Concerning.

n: Joseph must prepare his heart to receive and obey. Those to whom a law is revealed are accountable for it.

The Lord reveals a “new and everlasting covenant.” Rejecting it keeps one from God’s highest glory. In this section the phrase refers especially to eternal marriage, which is part of the fulness of the gospel covenant.

f.w: a new and an everlasting covenant

f.g: Stopped in progress; unable to receive the fullest blessings.

n: Every blessing comes by obeying the law God appointed for it before the world was made.

f.w: abide the law which was appointed for that blessing

n: The new and everlasting covenant is designed for the fulness of God’s glory; receiving that fulness requires keeping its law.

A key verse: any covenant or relationship not sealed by the Holy Spirit of Promise—through the one holding sealing keys—ends at death. Only one person at a time holds these keys on earth; today it is the President of the Church.

f.g: The Holy Ghost’s role in ratifying ordinances as valid in eternity, based on faithfulness.

f.w: there is never but one on the earth at a time
f.g: The President of the Church holds and directs all sealing keys.
Power to produce an effect.

n: God’s house is orderly, not confused.
Will God accept an offering not made in his name? The rhetorical question expects “no.”
Or receive something he hasn’t authorized?

f.w: that which I have not appointed

n: God appoints blessings only by law, as he and the Father ordained before the world.
No one comes to the Father except through Christ and his word—his law.

f.w: no man shall come unto the Father but by me

n: Everything not established by God—even human institutions and honors—will fall and not survive death or resurrection.
What God establishes endures; what he doesn’t will be shaken and destroyed.
So a marriage made only “until death” and not by God’s authority ends at death.

f.w: so long as he is in the world
f.g: Compare the common vow “till death do us part.”

n: After death such people neither marry nor are given in marriage—Jesus’ words—and serve as ministering angels to those who receive greater glory.

f.w: they neither marry nor are given in marriage

n: Not having kept this law, they remain single and separate, saved but not exalted—angels rather than gods.

f.g: Cannot grow into eternal family and increase.

n: Even a marriage meant to be eternal is not valid after death unless performed by God’s authority and sealed by the Holy Spirit of Promise. Heaven’s gatekeepers will not let it pass.

f.w: the angels and the gods are appointed there
f.g: Sentinels who admit only those properly sealed.

n: But a marriage done by God’s law, sealed by proper authority, and kept faithfully will endure: the couple will come forth in the resurrection and inherit thrones and kingdoms, with “a continuation of the seeds”—eternal posterity.

f.g: Eternal increase; the power to have posterity forever.

n: Such couples become gods—without end, above all, with all power. Latter-day Saints understand this as exaltation through Christ, always worshipping the Father and Son.
This glory cannot be reached without keeping this law.
Echoing Jesus: the gate is narrow, and few find the way to exaltation, because they don’t receive or know Christ.

f.w: strait is the gate, and narrow the way

f.g: Narrow, tight.

n: Receiving Christ in this life leads to truly knowing him and to exaltation—being where he is.

f.w: where I am ye shall be also

n: “Eternal lives” is knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ. The plural suggests the eternal family continuing.
The broad road leads to “the deaths”—the end of increase—because people do not receive Christ or his law.

f.w: Broad is the gate, and wide the way

n: A difficult verse: sealed persons who later sin seriously (short of murder) may still be exalted, but only after severe suffering—“destroyed in the flesh” and given to “the buffetings of Satan.” Church leaders have stressed that this is no license to sin and that repentance is still required.

f.g: Being left to Satan’s afflictions as a consequence of sin.

n: Blasphemy against the Holy Ghost—the unpardonable sin—includes shedding innocent blood and consenting to Christ’s death after having received this covenant.

f.w: The blasphemy against the Holy Ghost

n: The Lord will give Joseph the law of the priesthood ordained before the world.

f.w: the law of my Holy Priesthood
f.g: Here especially the laws governing sealing and eternal marriage.

n: Abraham received everything by revelation and is now exalted on his throne.
God promised Abraham descendants as countless as stars and sand—in this world and beyond. Joseph is among his seed.
The promise belongs to Joseph too, as Abraham’s seed. This law continues the Father’s work, by which he is glorified.
“Do the works of Abraham”—enter God’s law and be saved.
Those who don’t cannot receive the promise made to Abraham.
Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham as a wife, and from Hagar came many people (through Ishmael). The revelation presents this as part of fulfilling God’s promises.

f.w: Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham to wife

n: Was Abraham condemned? No, because God commanded it.

f.w: Verily I say unto you, Nay

n: Abraham was also commanded to offer Isaac, despite the command “Thou shalt not kill.” His obedience was counted as righteousness. God’s specific commands define what is right.

f.w: Abraham was commanded to offer his son Isaac
it was accounted unto him for righteousness

n: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob did only what they were commanded and are now exalted—gods, not angels.

f.w: they have entered into their exaltation

n: David, Solomon, Moses, and others had plural wives. They sinned only where they acted without God’s authorization.

f.w: save in those things which they received not of me

n: David’s wives were given through Nathan and other prophets; his only sin in this was with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah, for which he lost his exaltation.

f.w: in the case of Uriah and his wife

n: The Lord reminds Joseph he is appointed to restore all things.
Joseph had asked about adultery. A wife in this covenant who is with another man without divine authorization commits adultery.

f.g: Divine authorization through the sealing power.

n: A woman outside the covenant who is with another man also commits adultery. The moral law applies to all.
A husband under covenant who is with another woman breaks his vow and commits adultery. The standard applies to husbands too.
If a wife is innocent and the husband guilty, Joseph has authority by revelation to seal her to a faithful man.
Joseph holds the keys through which all things are restored.

f.w: the keys and power of the priesthood

n: The sealing power: what Joseph seals or binds on earth by God’s word is bound in heaven. Even remitting or retaining sins is included.

f.w: whatsoever you seal on earth shall be sealed in heaven

n: Those Joseph blesses, the Lord will bless—a promise also given to Abraham.

f.w: whomsoever you bless I will bless

n: Whatever Joseph does by God’s word and law will be blessed and without condemnation.
The Lord seals Joseph’s exaltation and prepares a throne for him with Abraham.

f.w: I seal upon you your exaltation

n: The Lord has seen Joseph’s sacrifices and forgives his sins, offering escape—as with Abraham, who was stopped from sacrificing Isaac.

f.w: as I accepted the offering of Abraham

n: Emma Smith is addressed. The meaning of this verse is uncertain; it seems to refer to some offer or test that the Lord now withdraws, “to prove you all,” as Abraham was tested.

f.g: Prove = test.

n: Emma is asked to accept the virtuous women sealed to Joseph. Historians note that this was extremely painful for Emma, who struggled with and at times opposed plural marriage.

f.w: receive all those that have been given unto my servant Joseph
f.g: Joseph was sealed to a number of women in Nauvoo; the details remain incompletely documented.

n: Joseph has been faithful in a few things and will be made ruler over many and strengthened.
Emma is commanded to stay with Joseph and no one else, with a severe warning if she does not abide God’s law.

f.g: Hold fast to; be faithful to.

n: If Emma doesn’t accept it, Joseph will still keep his promises to her, and the Lord will bless him a hundredfold—echoing Jesus’ promise to those who sacrifice.
Emma should forgive Joseph’s trespasses, and she will be forgiven and blessed with joy. Forgiveness in marriage runs both ways.

f.w: forgive my servant Joseph his trespasses

n: Joseph should not give away his property, lest enemies destroy him. Some suggest this relates to financial arrangements protecting Emma and the family.

f.w: put his property out of his hands
f.g: Transfer ownership of his property.

n: Now the Lord turns to more of the law of the priesthood.

f.w: there are many things pertaining thereunto
f.g: Indicates the revelation is only partial.

n: A man called of God as Aaron was, who acts by God’s word and keys, does not sin and will be justified.

f.w: called of my Father, as was Aaron

n: No one should attack Joseph; the Lord will justify him, and Joseph will offer the sacrifice required for his own transgressions.

f.g: Attack or oppose.

n: This verse describes plural marriage as practiced under divine authorization at that time, including the first wife’s consent. The Church discontinued plural marriage through the 1890 Manifesto; today only monogamous marriages are performed and anyone practicing polygamy cannot remain a member.

f.g: Marry, take as a spouse.

n: The revelation states that wives given by this law do not make the husband an adulterer, because they are lawfully his.

f.g: A number used for illustration, not a quota.

n: Such wives are given to “multiply and replenish the earth” and bear the souls of men, continuing the Father’s work. The verse states the stated purpose of the practice in that era.

f.g: Bring spirit children of God into mortal life.

n: If a wife taught this law rejects it, the verse warns of destruction. Historians and Church leaders acknowledge this teaching placed great strain on Emma and other women.

f.g: Support, assist.

n: If she does not receive the law, the husband may still receive what God gives him and is exempt from the “law of Sarah”—the pattern of a first wife consenting, as Sarah gave Hagar.
More will be revealed later. The Lord, Alpha and Omega, closes for now. Latter-day Saints today emphasize this section’s enduring teaching on eternal marriage and families.

f.w: I will reveal more unto you, hereafter
